speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: asked the Minister for Education whether the Government will review the policy regarding usage of the Post-Secondary Education Account (PSEA) to permit withdrawals for tertiary studies at private universities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Education)
text: This is because being part of the publicly-funded system, we are assured of the quality of the courses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Education)
text: Further, the programmes are already significantly subsidised and extending PSEA support is a natural thing to do.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Education)
text: We included other approved skills development programmes and modular courses that are subsidised by our continuing education and training policy and delivered by Government agencies and private training providers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Education)
text: Examples include the training programmes offered at the Building and Construction Authority (BCA) Academy and Digital Marketing in Hospitality offered at the Singapore Hotel Association Training and Education Centre (SHATEC) Institutes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Education)
text: If there is any unused amount in the PSEA when the account holder turns 30, this will be transferred to his or her Central Provident Fund (CPF) Ordinary Account (OA) in the following year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Education)
text: Quality and relevance remain the key considerations in deciding whether an education and training programme can qualify for PSEA usage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Education)
text: We need to protect the interests of account holders by ensuring that all courses eligible for PSEA support will meet quality standards and the needs of industries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Education)
text: While SkillsFuture Singapore regulates these private commercial players, they are not part of the public education system and we do not extend public subsidy to them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Education)
text: Likewise, we do not have a blanket policy to allow the usage of PSEA for their courses.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Speaker, four supplementary questions for Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, as the Senior Minister of State mentioned in his reply, any unused balance in the PSEA account will be transferred to the holder's CPF OA by the time he reaches 31.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The second question is, in his reply, I think he repeated the Ministry's stand that the restrictions on PSEA's use are due to concerns about quality as well as relevance.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We have come across some residents who had appealed to use PSEA for degree programmes offered by foreign universities that have good international reputation and, in fact, who have collaborations within Singapore with polytechnics and, in one case, an aeronautical university that has a collaboration with the Air Force.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, would the Senior Minister of State agree that such collaborations are signs that there is an acceptance of the quality of the university offering those degrees and, in a sense, also of the relevance of studies in such fields, that is why there are collaborations in Singapore?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The third question is, the Senior Minister of State mentioned also that PSEA is only allowed for Government-subsidised programmes as a natural consequence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Would he not agree that in the sense there is a certain perversion in that logic because a person with less resources would need a support if there is a lack of subsidies in that sense?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, I think that reason is not that convincing.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, what is the relevance of the EduTrust mark?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is it not also a sign of quality assurance?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But if the Member could file a separate Parliamentary Question, we would provide the information to her separately.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As for the other questions from Ms Sylvia Lim, she first asked about the collaborations of different programmes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think I have explained this in my answer, which is, that we look at both the quality and also the relevance.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Some of these programmes that the Membe mentioned are offered by foreign universities.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We understand there is a range of courses offered globally.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But it would not be possible for the Ministry of Education to maintain a comprehensive list of approved overseas programmes because we do need to safeguard the usage of PSEA monies.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For practical reasons, it is limited to local institutions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, if you have a foreign university but they have a local institution and they run some programmes here, as I explained in my answer, some of them do qualify for Continuing Education and Training (CET) funding.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We are looking at the range of possible courses but based on the criteria of quality and also industry relevance.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Ms Sylvia Lim also said that she has some disagreement with the explanation about quality because these courses are not given subsidy, therefore, we should be allowing the students to use PSEA.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think we have to look at what is the objective that we are trying to achieve in the first place.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If you look at the quality of the programme, there is a reason why they are not receiving public subsidy.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, because of this, it is not possible to use this approach to say that just because a programme is not subsidised, therefore, you should allow students to use their PSEA.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In fact, if you agree that quality of a course and the relevance of the course and the outcomes that the graduates are able to achieve are important considerations, then we should, first and foremost, be looking at what is the quality of this course and does it offer students good employment outcomes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In the end, we should not forget that the student has to put in considerable amounts of resources, both time and money, to be able to attend and complete the course.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, if the outcomes are not good, I do not think we should be sending mixed signals to confuse people that they are encouraged to sign up for this course when the outcomes are actually not very desirable.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think we do have an obligation and duty to signal clearly to students who are looking at options to consider what are the outcomes and, therefore, please think carefully before you decide.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Going to a PEI is not the only option for someone who has completed GCE "A" level or polytechnic.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is not the only means for young Singaporeans to be work-ready.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have very good employment outcomes for Polytechnic Diploma graduates and, for many of them, after they join the workforce, there are still opportunities available for them to do their degrees on a part-time basis or on a full-time basis subsequently after they have started working.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have also introduced new pathways, including the post-Diploma Advanced or Specialist Diploma for polytechnic students and the Work-Study Diploma and Post-Diploma pathways that are now available to our students in ITE or polytechnics.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These are applied programmes that combine structured on-the-job training and institution-based courses.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The good thing is that when they are under this programme, the Earn-and-Learn programme or the Work-Study Programme, they can earn a salary while they are working and also go back to school.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For the students who are doing the Advanced or Specialist Diploma, it takes up to 18 months.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For the new pathway that we introduced, where students would pursue a Work-Study programme leading to a Degree, it will take about three years for polytechnic students.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, it is important that we provide our students with a good understanding of what are the options, what are the pathways and what are the outcomes of the different pathways so that parents and students are better able to make good decisions on how they want to commit their time and resources.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is about whether the governance, administration and the fee protection, whether these elements are adequately provided.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: More to protect students from cases where, like in the past, some of the PEIs folded halfway through the course and the students were then left in the lurch because the money that they had paid, they could not get it back.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, EduTrust is meant more for that purpose.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It does not say anything about the quality of the course or the industry relevance or even the outcomes for the graduates.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think we should separate the two and not mix them up.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Getting EduTrust does not mean that you have good outcomes for your students.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But I also mentioned in my reply that we do have private providers that we have allowed to qualify for subsidies.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Let us not make classifications based on what type of entity you are as the main focus of our efforts.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Let us look at the quality of the courses, the relevance to the industry and the outcomes to the graduates.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: [Pursuant to Standing Order No 22(3), provided that Members had not asked for questions standing in their names to be postponed to a later Sitting day or withdrawn, written answers to questions not reached by the end of Question Time are reproduced in the Appendix.]
